{{short description|Mathematical function}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''prime zeta function''' is an analogue of the [[Riemann zeta function]], studied by {{harvtxt|Glaisher|1891}}. It is defined as the following [[infinite series]], which converges for {{tmath| \Re(s) > 1 }}:
: <math>P(s)=\sum_{p\,\in\mathrm{\,primes}} \frac{1}{p^s}=\frac{1}{2^s}+\frac{1}{3^s}+\frac{1}{5^s}+\frac{1}{7^s}+\frac{1}{11^s}+\dots\ .</math>

== Properties ==

The [[Euler product]] for the  Riemann zeta function <math>\zeta(s)</math> implies that
: <math>\log\zeta(s)=\sum_{n>0} \frac{P(ns)} n ,</math>
which by [[Möbius inversion]] gives
: <math>P(s)=\sum_{n>0} \mu(n)\frac{\log\zeta(ns)} n</math>

When <math>s</math> goes to 1, we have {{tmath| \textstyle P(s) \sim \log\zeta(s)\sim\log\left(\frac{1}{s-1} \right) }}.
This is used in the definition of [[Dirichlet density]].

This gives the continuation of <math>P(s)</math> to {{tmath| \Re(s) > 0 }}, with an infinite number of logarithmic singularities at points <math>s</math> where <math>ns</math> is a pole (only <math>ns=1</math> when <math>n</math> is a squarefree number greater than or equal to 1), or zero of the  Riemann zeta function ''ζ''('''.'''). The line <math>\Re(s) = 0</math> is a natural boundary as the singularities cluster near all points of this line.

If one defines a sequence
: <math>a_n=\prod_{p^k \mid n} \frac{1}{k}=\prod_{p^k \mid \mid n} \frac 1 {k!} </math>
then
: <math>P(s)=\log\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{a_n}{n^s}.</math>

(Exponentiation shows that this is equivalent to Lemma 2.7 by Li.)

The prime zeta function is related to [[Artin's constant]] by
: <math>\ln C_{\mathrm{Artin}} = - \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{(L_n-1)P(n)}{n} </math>
where <math>L_n</math> is the {{tmath| n }}th [[Lucas number]].<ref>{{MathWorld|ArtinsConstant|Artin's Constant}}</ref>

== Analysis ==

=== Integral ===

The integral over the prime zeta function is usually anchored at infinity, because the pole at <math>s=1</math> prohibits defining a nice lower bound at some finite [[integer]] without entering a discussion on branch cuts in the [[complex plane]]:
: <math>\int_s^\infty P(t) \, dt = \sum_p \frac 1 {p^s\log p}</math>

The noteworthy values are again those where the sums converge slowly:

{| class="wikitable sortable"
! <math>s</math> !! approximate value <math>\sum _p 1/(p^s\log p)</math> !! [[OEIS]]
|-
| 1 || <math>1.63661632\ldots</math> || {{OEIS2C|A137245}}
|-
| 2 || <math>0.50778218\ldots</math> || {{OEIS2C|A221711}}
|-
| 3 || <math>0.22120334\ldots</math> ||
|-
| 4 || <math>0.10266547\ldots</math> ||
|}

=== Derivative ===
The first derivative is
: <math>P'(s) \equiv \frac{d}{ds} P(s) = - \sum_p \frac{\log p}{p^s}</math>

The interesting values are again those where the sums converge slowly:

{| class="wikitable sortable"
! <math>s</math> !!approximate value <math>P'(s)</math> !! [[OEIS]]
|-
| 2 || <math>-0.493091109\ldots</math> || {{OEIS2C|A136271}}
|-
| 3 || <math>-0.150757555\ldots</math> || {{OEIS2C|A303493}}
|-
| 4 || <math>-0.060607633\ldots</math> || {{OEIS2C|A303494}}
|-
| 5 || <math>-0.026838601\ldots</math> || {{OEIS2C|A303495}}
|}

== Generalizations ==

=== Almost-prime zeta functions ===
As the Riemann zeta function is a sum of inverse powers over the integers and the prime zeta function a sum of inverse powers of the prime numbers, the <math>k</math>-primes (the integers that are a product of <math>k</math> not necessarily distinct primes) define a sort of intermediate sums:
: <math>P_k(s)\equiv \sum_{n: \Omega(n)=k} \frac 1 {n^s} ,</math>
where <math>\Omega</math> is the total number of [[prime factor]]s.

{| class="wikitable sortable"
! <math>k</math> !! <math>s</math> !! approximate value <math>P_k(s)</math>!![[OEIS]]
|-
| 2 || 2 || <math>0.14076043434\ldots</math> || {{OEIS2C|A117543}}
|-
| 2 || 3 || <math>0.02380603347\ldots</math> ||
|-
| 3 || 2 || <math>0.03851619298\ldots</math> || {{OEIS2C|A131653}}
|-
| 3 || 3 || <math>0.00304936208\ldots</math> ||
|}

Each integer in the denominator of the Riemann zeta function <math>\zeta</math> may be classified by its value of the index {{tmath| k }}, which decomposes the Riemann zeta function into an infinite sum of the {{tmath| P_k }}:
: <math>\zeta(s) = 1+\sum_{k=1,2,\ldots} P_k(s)</math>

Since we know that the [[Prime_omega_function#Dirichlet_series|Dirichlet series]] (in some formal parameter {{tmath| u }}) satisfies 
: <math>P_{\Omega}(u, s) := \sum_{n \geq 1} \frac{u^{\Omega(n)}}{n^s} = \prod_{p \in \mathbb{P}} \left(1-up^{-s}\right)^{-1},</math>
we can use formulas for the [[Complete_homogeneous_symmetric_polynomial|symmetric polynomial variants]] with a [[generating function]] of the right-hand-side type. Namely, we have the coefficient-wise identity that <math>P_k(s) = [u^k] P_{\Omega}(u, s) = h(x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots)</math> when the sequences correspond to <math>x_j := j^{-s} \chi_{\mathbb{P}}(j)</math> where <math>\chi_{\mathbb{P}}</math> denotes the characteristic function of the [[prime numbers|primes]]. Using [[Newton%27s_identities#Expressing_complete_homogeneous_symmetric_polynomials_in_terms_of_power_sums|Newton's identities]], we have a general formula for these sums given by 
: <math>P_n(s) = \sum_{{k_1+2k_2+\cdots+nk_n=n} \atop {k_1,\ldots,k_n \geq 0}} \left[\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{P(is)^{k_i}}{k_i! \cdot i^{k_i}}\right] = -[z^n]\log\left(1 - \sum_{j \geq 1} \frac{P(js) z^j}{j}\right).</math> 

Special cases include the following explicit expansions:
: <math>\begin{align}P_1(s) & = P(s) \\ P_2(s) & = \frac{1}{2}\left(P(s)^2+P(2s)\right) \\ P_3(s) & = \frac{1}{6}\left(P(s)^3+3P(s)P(2s)+2P(3s)\right) \\ P_4(s) & = \frac{1}{24}\left(P(s)^4+6P(s)^2 P(2s)+3 P(2s)^2+8P(s)P(3s)+6P(4s)\right).\end{align}</math>

=== Prime modulo zeta functions ===
Constructing the sum not over all primes but only over primes that are in the same modulo class introduces further types of infinite series that are a reduction of the [[Dirichlet L-function]].
